sections.h: 波長と光子エネルギーの関係
sections.p: 光子1個のエネルギーは E = hν = hc/λ で、波長が短いほど大きくなります。電子ボルト(eV)とナノメートル(nm)で表すと E[eV] ≈ 1239.84/λ[nm] となり、「1240をナノメートルの波長で割るとeV」と覚えておくと便利です。既定値の1550 nmでは約0.80 eV、可視光の緑(530 nm)では約2.34 eV、紫外線の365 nmでは約3.40 eVです。半導体の受光素子や光源では、バンドギャップと光子エネルギーを比べることで、その波長を吸収・発光できるかが分かります。

周波数は ν = c/λ で、1550 nmは約193.4 THzです。光通信の波長多重(DWDM)では、波長ではなく周波数で193.1 THzを中心とした50 GHzや100 GHzの間隔のチャネルを定めています。1550 nm付近では100 GHzが約0.8 nmにあたります。波数(cm⁻¹)は1 cmあたりの波の数で、1/λを cm⁻¹ で表したものです。赤外分光やラマン分光ではこの単位が標準で、1550 nmは約6452 cm⁻¹です。
光パワーPを光子1個のエネルギーで割ると、1秒あたりの光子数 N = P/(hν) が得られます。1550 nm・1 mWでは約7.80 × 10¹⁵ 個/s です。同じパワーでも、波長が長いほど光子1個のエネルギーが小さいので、光子の数は多くなります。ショット雑音や単一光子検出を考えるときは、この光子の数が基本になります。

受光素子の応答度は R = η·qλ/(hc) で、量子効率ηが100 %のとき R[A/W] ≈ λ[nm]/1239.84 となります。1550 nmでは上限が約1.25 A/W、850 nmでは約0.686 A/Wです。実際のInGaAsフォトダイオードの1550 nmでの応答度は0.9〜1.0 A/W程度で、量子効率に直すと70〜80 %程度です。応答度が波長に比例するのは、同じパワーでも長波長ほど光子の数が多いためです。

faq.q: eV から nm に換算するには?
faq.a: λ[nm] ≈ 1239.84/E[eV] で計算します。たとえばシリコンのバンドギャップ1.12 eVは約1107 nm、GaNの3.4 eVは約365 nmです。

faq.q: 物質の中では光子エネルギーは変わりますか?
faq.a: 変わりません。屈折率nの物質の中では光の速さと波長が1/nになりますが、周波数と光子エネルギーはそのままです。この計算機の波長は真空中の値として扱っています。

faq.q: 1550 nm と 1310 nm の光子エネルギーは?
faq.a: 1550 nmは約0.800 eV(約193.4 THz)、1310 nmは約0.946 eV(約228.8 THz)です。どちらもシリコンのバンドギャップ(約1.12 eV)より小さいので、シリコンでは吸収されず、受光にはInGaAsやGeが使われます。

en.card: Convert between wavelength, frequency, photon energy (eV) and wavenumber
en.title: Wavelength to Photon Energy Converter: nm, THz, eV and cm⁻¹
en.description: Convert light between wavelength (nm), frequency (THz), photon energy (eV) and wavenumber (cm⁻¹). From optical power, it also calculates photons per second and the responsivity of an ideal photodetector at 100% quantum efficiency.
en.h1: Wavelength, Frequency and Photon Energy Converter
en.lead: Edit any one field and the others are converted. Enter an optical power to see how many photons arrive per second and the responsivity of an ideal photodetector. The defaults are 1550 nm, in the C band used for optical communications.
en.note: Wavelengths are treated as vacuum values (inside a material the wavelength becomes 1/n, but frequency and photon energy do not change). Constants: c = 299,792,458 m/s, h = 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, e = 1.602176634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

sections.p: The energy of one photon is E = hν = hc/λ, larger at shorter wavelengths. In electronvolts (eV) and nanometers (nm), E[eV] ≈ 1239.84/λ[nm]; a handy rule is “1240 divided by the wavelength in nanometers gives eV”. The default 1550 nm is about 0.80 eV, visible green (530 nm) about 2.34 eV, and ultraviolet at 365 nm about 3.40 eV. For semiconductor photodetectors and light sources, comparing the band gap with the photon energy tells you whether that wavelength can be absorbed or emitted.

Frequency is ν = c/λ, and 1550 nm is about 193.4 THz. Dense wavelength-division multiplexing (DWDM) in optical communications defines its channels by frequency rather than wavelength, with 50 GHz or 100 GHz spacing centered on 193.1 THz. Near 1550 nm, 100 GHz corresponds to about 0.8 nm. Wavenumber (cm⁻¹) is the number of waves per centimeter, 1/λ expressed in cm⁻¹. It is the standard unit in infrared and Raman spectroscopy; 1550 nm is about 6452 cm⁻¹.

Dividing optical power P by the energy of one photon gives the number of photons per second, N = P/(hν). For 1 mW at 1550 nm, it is about 7.80 × 10¹⁵ photons/s. At the same power, longer wavelengths have less energy per photon and therefore more photons. This photon count is the starting point when considering shot noise or single-photon detection.

The responsivity of a photodetector is R = η·qλ/(hc), and with a quantum efficiency η of 100%, R[A/W] ≈ λ[nm]/1239.84. The upper limit is about 1.25 A/W at 1550 nm and about 0.686 A/W at 850 nm. Real InGaAs photodiodes have a responsivity of roughly 0.9–1.0 A/W at 1550 nm, which corresponds to a quantum efficiency of about 70–80%. Responsivity is proportional to wavelength because, at the same power, longer wavelengths carry more photons.

faq.q: How do I convert eV to nm?
faq.a: Use λ[nm] ≈ 1239.84/E[eV]. For example, silicon's band gap of 1.12 eV corresponds to about 1107 nm, and GaN's 3.4 eV to about 365 nm.

faq.q: Does photon energy change inside a material?
faq.a: No. In a material with refractive index n, the speed and wavelength of light become 1/n of their vacuum values, but the frequency and photon energy stay the same. This calculator treats wavelengths as vacuum values.

faq.q: What are the photon energies at 1550 nm and 1310 nm?
faq.a: 1550 nm is about 0.800 eV (about 193.4 THz) and 1310 nm about 0.946 eV (about 228.8 THz). Both are below silicon's band gap (about 1.12 eV), so silicon does not absorb them, and InGaAs or Ge is used for detection.
